# Theory study guide

Everything to learn for the theory demos, in one document, in the order to study it:
the open sub-goals of *App Deployment (Basic)*, *App Deployment (Intermediate)* and *Multiply productivity using AI*.

About 24,000 words: roughly 2 hours of reading, longer with the exercises.
Each part stands on its own, so it can be read one sitting at a time.

The debugging demo is live, not theory, so it is not in here. Its runbook is [debugging-demo.md](debugging-demo.md).

## How to use this guide

Every sub-topic is laid out the same way, so you always know where to look:

1. **In one sentence:** the whole idea, short enough to open with.
2. **Why it matters:** what goes wrong without it.
3. **Key ideas:** the terms you need, in plain words.
4. **Try it yourself:** safe commands to run on your own machine (Docker is already set up), so the
   theory sticks. Nothing here changes production; a few read-only checks look at the live site.
5. **In this project:** where Seat Planner already does it, with the files to open.
6. **At larger scale:** what bigger teams use instead or as well.
7. **Common mistakes:** the usual traps, and how to avoid them.
8. **Explain it in two minutes:** a short talk to give in the demo.
9. **Questions you may be asked:** with answers.

Jenkins and the AI goal leave out the parts that do not fit. The first three Jenkins sub-topics have no
exercises (two have a worked example instead), and the AI sub-topics draw on this project's own history
instead of *At larger scale* and *Common mistakes*.

When you present:

- Open with the **one sentence**, then the **why**: people remember the problem better than the term.
- Use **this project** as your example wherever you can. It is real, it runs, and you know it.
- Say plainly what this project does **not** do yet, and what you would add. It sounds honest, and it
  shows you understand the topic, not just the tool.
- Keep the **Try it yourself** commands in your pocket: if asked "how would you check that?", you can
  answer with the command.

The same material is also in separate pages, one per part, in this folder ([index](README.md)). This document
is built from them, so the two always match.

## Part 1: Docker basics

Goal: **App Deployment (Basic)**. Three sub-goals, each at 50%: [Basic commands](#basic-commands),
[Networking](#networking), [Debugging and logs](#debugging-and-logs).

The project already uses Docker (that was the first 50%). This part fills in the rest: the commands
behind it, how the containers find each other, and how to find out what went wrong.

> **Where to type the commands:** use **PowerShell**. Git Bash rewrites anything that looks like a
> Linux path (`/usr/share/...` becomes `C:/Program Files/Git/usr/share/...`) and has trouble with
> `-it`. If you do use Git Bash, start the line with `MSYS_NO_PATHCONV=1` and put `winpty` before
> `docker ... -it`.
>
> Every exercise uses its own throw-away containers (`hello`, `web`, `broken`...). The project's
> running `seat-planner-mongo-1` is only ever **looked at**, never stopped or removed.

### Basic commands

#### In one sentence

An **image** is a frozen, ready-to-run copy of an app and everything it needs; a **container** is
one running copy of that image; a handful of commands builds, starts, inspects, stops and removes them.

#### Why it matters

"It works on my machine" happens because machines differ: Node version, operating system, a missing
library. An image carries all of that with it, so the same image runs the same way on your laptop,
in CI and on the server. The commands are how you drive it; without them Docker is a black box.

#### Key ideas

| Term | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **Image** | A read-only package: a small Linux, the runtime (Node 20), your code, its libraries, and the command to start it. Built from a `Dockerfile`. |
| **Layer** | Each line of a Dockerfile adds a layer on top of the last. Unchanged layers are reused from cache, which is why rebuilds can be fast. |
| **Container** | A running (or stopped) copy of an image, with its own files, process list and network address. Many containers can come from one image. |
| **Tag** | A name for an image version: `node:20-alpine`, `mysql:8`. Without a tag Docker assumes `:latest`. |
| **Registry** | A server that stores images. Docker Hub is the default; `docker pull` downloads from it. |
| **Volume** | Storage that lives outside the container, so data survives when the container is removed. |
| **Port mapping** | `-p 8080:80` means "traffic to port 8080 on my machine goes to port 80 in the container". |
| **Docker Compose** | One YAML file that describes several containers and starts them together. |

**The commands you need, grouped by what they do:**

| Job | Command | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Get an image | `docker pull nginx:alpine` | `run` pulls automatically if missing |
| Build an image | `docker build -t myapp:1.0 .` | `.` is the *build context*: the folder sent to Docker |
| List images | `docker images` | |
| Start a container | `docker run -d --name hello -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine` | `-d` runs it in the background |
| List containers | `docker ps` (running) · `docker ps -a` (all, stopped too) | |
| Stop / start / restart | `docker stop hello` · `docker start hello` · `docker restart hello` | `stop` asks politely (SIGTERM), then forces after 10 s |
| Run a command inside | `docker exec -it hello sh` | Alpine images have `sh`, not `bash` |
| Read its output | `docker logs hello` | See [Debugging and logs](#debugging-and-logs) |
| Remove | `docker rm hello` · `docker rm -f hello` (even if running) · `docker rmi nginx:alpine` | |
| See disk use | `docker system df` | |
| Clean up unused things | `docker system prune` | Asks first. **Never** add `--volumes` unless you mean to delete data |

**Flags worth knowing on `docker run`:** `-d` (background), `--name` (a name you choose), `-p host:container`
(publish a port), `-e KEY=value` (an environment variable), `-v name:/path` (attach a volume),
`--rm` (delete the container when it stops), `-it` (an interactive terminal).

**Compose versions of the same:**

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| `docker compose up -d --build` | Build what needs building, start everything in the background |
| `docker compose ps` | The project's containers and their state |
| `docker compose logs -f backend` | Follow one service's output |
| `docker compose exec backend sh` | A shell inside the running backend |
| `docker compose stop` | Stop, keep the containers |
| `docker compose down` | Stop and remove the containers and network; **volumes (data) are kept** |
| `docker compose down -v` | The same, **and delete the volumes: the database is gone** |

#### Try it yourself

```powershell
docker pull nginx:alpine                          # download a small web server image
docker images                                     # it is listed, with its size
docker run -d --name hello -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
docker ps                                         # running; PORTS shows 0.0.0.0:8080->80/tcp
curl.exe http://localhost:8080                    # the nginx welcome page (or open it in a browser)
docker logs hello                                 # one line per request you just made
docker exec -it hello sh                          # now you are INSIDE the container
  ls /usr/share/nginx/html                        #   the files it serves
  cat /etc/os-release                             #   it is Alpine Linux, not Windows
  exit
docker stop hello ; docker ps -a                  # stopped, not gone: STATUS says Exited (0)
docker start hello                                # same container again, same name
docker rm -f hello                                # gone
docker rmi nginx:alpine                           # image removed too
```

Then look, without touching, at the project's own container:

```powershell
docker ps --filter name=seat-planner              # seat-planner-mongo-1, Up ... days
docker system df                                  # how much space images, containers and volumes use
```

#### In this project

- [`backend/Dockerfile`](../../backend/Dockerfile): every line is commented. Read it top to bottom once;
  it is the clearest summary of what an image is.
- [`frontend/Dockerfile`](../../frontend/Dockerfile): a two-stage build (covered in
  [Docker, advanced](#optimizing-images)).
- [`docker-compose.yml`](../../docker-compose.yml): five services (`db`, `mongo`, `backend`, `frontend`,
  `caddy`) and four volumes.
- [`README.md`, "Everything in Docker"](../../README.md#everything-in-docker): `docker compose up --build`,
  then `docker compose exec backend npm run seed:superadmin`.
- Day to day only MongoDB runs in Docker: `docker compose up -d mongo`. The API and web app run
  directly with Node, which is faster to restart while coding.
- In production, Render builds `backend/Dockerfile` itself on every deploy and runs the container.

#### At larger scale

Nobody types `docker run` on production servers. A CI pipeline builds and tags the image, pushes it to a
registry, and an orchestrator (Kubernetes, Amazon ECS, or a platform like Render) pulls and runs it.
The commands above are still what you use to reproduce a problem on your own machine.

#### Common mistakes

- **`docker compose down -v` "to start fresh"** deletes every database volume. Use plain `down`.
- **Using `:latest`** for real deployments. It changes under you; pin a version (`mysql:8`, `node:20-alpine`).
- **Forgetting `-d`** and then closing the terminal, which stops the container.
- **Editing files inside a running container** with `exec`. The change is lost when the container is
  recreated. Change the source and rebuild.
- **`docker system prune -a --volumes`** copied from the internet. It removes every unused image and volume.

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "A Docker image is a package with our code, Node 20 and a small Linux inside. A container is that
> image running. In this project the API's [Dockerfile](../../backend/Dockerfile) starts from
> `node:20-alpine`, copies `package.json` first so the `npm ci` step is cached, copies the code, switches
> to a non-root user, and starts with `npm run migrate && npm start`. Render builds that same file on
> every deploy, so what runs in production is exactly what I can run here.
>
> The day-to-day commands are `build`, `run`, `ps`, `logs`, `exec`, `stop` and `rm`. With Compose the same
> verbs work on the whole stack: `docker compose up -d --build` starts MySQL, MongoDB, the API, the web
> app and the Caddy proxy together. One thing I am careful with: `down` keeps the data, `down -v`
> deletes it."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **What is the difference between an image and a container?** An image is the read-only template; a
  container is a running instance of it, with its own writable layer on top. One image, many containers.
- **`docker stop` vs `docker kill`?** `stop` sends SIGTERM, waits 10 seconds, then SIGKILL. `kill` sends
  SIGKILL straight away, so the app gets no chance to finish.
- **`CMD` vs `ENTRYPOINT`?** `ENTRYPOINT` is the fixed program; `CMD` is the default arguments, which
  `docker run image <something>` replaces. This project only uses `CMD`.
- **`COPY` vs `ADD`?** Use `COPY`. `ADD` also unpacks archives and downloads URLs, which surprises people.
- **What does `EXPOSE` do?** Nothing at run time; it documents the port. `-p` (or `ports:` in Compose)
  actually publishes it.
- **Where does a container's data go when it is removed?** Gone, unless it was in a volume. That is
  why MySQL writes to the `db_data` volume.

### Networking

#### In one sentence

Docker gives each container its own network address and puts the containers of one Compose project on a
private network where they find each other **by service name**; only the ports you publish can be
reached from outside.

#### Why it matters

Most "it cannot connect" problems in Docker are networking mistakes: using `localhost` in the wrong
place, publishing a database to the whole network by accident, or containers on different networks.
Knowing the rules turns those from hours into minutes.

#### Key ideas

| Term | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **Network namespace** | Each container has its own network stack. `localhost` inside a container means **that container**, not your PC. |
| **Bridge network** | A private virtual network on your machine. The default type. |
| **User-defined network** | A bridge network you (or Compose) create. It has **built-in DNS**: containers reach each other by name. The original default `bridge` network does not. |
| **Service discovery** | Finding a service by name instead of IP. In Compose the service name (`db`, `mongo`, `backend`) is the host name. |
| **Publishing a port** | `-p 8080:80` / `ports:` opens a door from your machine into the container. Without it the container is reachable only from its own network. |
| **Bind address** | `127.0.0.1:27017:27017` publishes on your machine only. `27017:27017` publishes on **every** network card, so other computers on the Wi-Fi can reach it. |
| **`host.docker.internal`** | A name Docker Desktop provides so a container can reach a program running on your PC. |
| **Other drivers** | `host` (share the PC's network, Linux only), `none` (no network), `overlay` (across several machines, for Swarm/Kubernetes-style clusters). |

The picture for this project:

```text
your browser ──▶ :80 / :443 ──▶ caddy ──┬── /api/* ──▶ backend:4000 ──┬──▶ db:3306      (MySQL, not published)
                (published)              │                              └──▶ mongo:27017  (MongoDB)
                                         └── else ───▶ frontend:3000
                                                                            127.0.0.1:27017 ──▶ mongo
                                                                            (published to this PC only)
                       all five on the private network  seat-planner_default
```

#### Try it yourself

**1. Names work on a user-defined network, not on the default one:**

```powershell
docker network create demo-net
docker run -d --name web --network demo-net nginx:alpine
docker run --rm --network demo-net alpine wget -qO- http://web    # HTML: "web" was found by name
docker run --rm alpine wget -qO- -T 3 http://web                  # fails: "bad address 'web'" (default bridge, no DNS)
docker network inspect demo-net                                    # "Containers": web, with its IP
docker rm -f web ; docker network rm demo-net
```

**2. `localhost` inside a container is the container itself:**

```powershell
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
docker run --rm alpine wget -qO- -T 3 http://localhost:8080              # "Connection refused": nothing listens on 8080 in THIS container
docker run --rm alpine wget -qO- -T 3 http://host.docker.internal:8080   # works: goes out to your PC, back in through -p
docker rm -f web
```

**3. Look at the project's network (read-only):**

```powershell
docker network ls                                   # seat-planner_default is there
docker network inspect seat-planner_default         # mongo's IP on it
docker port seat-planner-mongo-1                    # 27017/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:27017
```

#### In this project

- [`docker-compose.yml`](../../docker-compose.yml) never writes an IP address. The backend is told
  `DB_HOST: db` and `MONGO_URI: mongodb://mongo:27017/seat_planner`; Compose's DNS does the rest.
- [`Caddyfile`](../../Caddyfile): `reverse_proxy backend:4000` and `reverse_proxy frontend:3000`, again by name.
  Caddy is the **single entry point**; it is the only service with public ports (80 and 443).
- **MySQL has no `ports:` at all**, so nothing outside the Compose network can reach it.
- **MongoDB is published on `127.0.0.1` only**, with a comment explaining why: it has no password, so it
  must not be reachable from the rest of the network. The port exists so the API, run directly with
  Node during development, can use it.
- The web image is built with `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL=/api`, a **relative** address, so the same image
  works behind any domain: the proxy decides where `/api` goes.
- In production the same idea holds across services: Vercel rewrites `/api/*` to the Render API, and the
  API reaches Aiven MySQL over TLS by host name.

#### At larger scale

Kubernetes keeps the same model with different names: a **Service** gives a stable name and address to
a group of containers, an **Ingress** (or gateway) is the single entry point like Caddy, and **network
policies** say which services may talk to which. Across several machines the network is an *overlay*.

#### Common mistakes

- **`DB_HOST=localhost` in a container.** It points at the container itself. Use the service name.
- **Publishing a database with `"3306:3306"`.** That is every network interface. On a Linux server Docker
  also adds its own firewall rules, which can bypass `ufw`. Do not publish it, or bind to `127.0.0.1`.
- **Mixing up the two port numbers.** `-p HOST:CONTAINER`. The app listens on the container's port;
  you browse to the host's port.
- **The app listening on `127.0.0.1` inside the container.** Then nothing outside it can connect, even
  with `-p`. It must listen on `0.0.0.0`. (That is why the web image sets `HOSTNAME=0.0.0.0`.)
- **Containers in different Compose projects** cannot see each other by name unless you attach them to a
  shared network.

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "Compose creates a private network for the project, `seat-planner_default`, and every service joins it.
> On that network each service name is a host name, so the API connects to `db` for MySQL and `mongo`
> for MongoDB, and Caddy forwards to `backend:4000` and `frontend:3000`. There is not a single IP address
> in the configuration.
>
> From outside, only what is published can be reached. Caddy publishes 80 and 443 and is the one door
> in. MySQL is not published at all. MongoDB is published only on 127.0.0.1, because it has no password
> and should never be visible to the office network. The one trap everyone hits once: inside a container,
> `localhost` is that container, so you use the service name, or `host.docker.internal` to reach your own PC."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **How do two containers talk to each other?** Put them on the same user-defined network and use the
  container or service name. Compose does this automatically.
- **Why can't containers on the default `bridge` network use names?** The default bridge has no built-in
  DNS; only user-defined networks have it. (`--link` was the old workaround; it is deprecated.)
- **What is the difference between `EXPOSE` and `-p`?** `EXPOSE` documents; `-p` publishes.
- **How would you check whether a container can reach another?** `docker exec -it <a> sh`, then
  `wget -qO- http://<b>:<port>` or `nc -zv <b> <port>`; and `docker network inspect` to see who is on which network.
- **What does the `host` network driver do?** The container uses the machine's network directly, no
  isolation and no port mapping. Linux only; rarely needed.

### Debugging and logs

#### In one sentence

When a container misbehaves you read what it printed (`docker logs`), check how it ended (`docker ps -a`,
`docker inspect`), and, if it is still running, look inside it (`docker exec`), in that order.

#### Why it matters

A container that exits straight away, restarts forever or "cannot connect" gives no error on screen.
The answer is almost always in its logs or its exit code; you just need to know where to look.

#### Key ideas

| Term | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **stdout / stderr** | The two output streams of a program. Docker captures both and keeps them as the container's log. |
| **Log driver** | Where Docker stores those logs. The default, `json-file`, keeps them in a file per container, **with no size limit** unless you set one. |
| **Exit code** | The number a program ends with. `0` = fine, `1` = the app reported an error, `137` = killed (SIGKILL, often **out of memory**), `143` = stopped by SIGTERM, `127` = command not found. |
| **Restart policy** | `restart: unless-stopped` makes Docker restart a crashed container. Good for uptime, but a crash loop then looks like "Up 2 seconds". |
| **Healthcheck** | A command Docker runs every few seconds to ask "are you ready?". State is `starting`, `healthy` or `unhealthy`. |
| **`docker inspect`** | Everything Docker knows about a container as JSON: state, exit code, OOM flag, environment, mounts, networks, health. |
| **`docker events`** | A live feed of what Docker is doing: start, die, kill, oom, health_status. |
| **`docker stats`** | Live CPU, memory and network per container, like Task Manager. |

**Where to look, in order:**

1. `docker ps -a`: is it running, restarting, or exited, and with what code?
2. `docker logs <name> --tail 100`: the last thing it said.
3. `docker inspect <name>`: why it stopped (`State.ExitCode`, `State.OOMKilled`, `State.Error`), and
   what it was given (environment, mounts, network).
4. `docker exec -it <name> sh`: look around inside, if it stays up long enough.
5. If it dies too fast to `exec`: start the image with a shell instead of its normal command:
   `docker run -it --rm --entrypoint sh <image>` (or `docker compose run --rm backend sh`), then run the
   start command by hand and watch it fail.

**`docker logs` options:** `-f` follow, `--tail 100` last lines, `--since 10m` time window, `-t` add
timestamps. The Compose form `docker compose logs -f backend` merges and colours several services.

#### Try it yourself

**1. A container that fails, and how to find out why:**

```powershell
docker run --name broken alpine sh -c "echo starting; echo 'cannot read config' >&2; exit 3"
docker ps -a --filter name=broken                         # Exited (3)
docker logs broken                                        # both lines: stdout and stderr
docker inspect broken --format "{{.State.ExitCode}}"      # 3
docker rm broken
```

**2. Killed for running out of memory (exit code 137):**

```powershell
docker run --name oom -m 32m alpine sh -c "tail /dev/zero"     # eats memory until stopped
docker inspect oom --format "{{.State.ExitCode}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}}"   # 137 OOMKilled=true
docker rm oom
```

**3. Following logs live, with timestamps, and watching events in a second window:**

```powershell
# window 1
docker events --filter type=container
# window 2
docker run -d --name hello -p 8080:80 nginx:alpine
curl.exe http://localhost:8080 ; curl.exe http://localhost:8080/nope
docker logs -f -t --tail 5 hello            # a 200 and a 404, with times; Ctrl+C to stop following
docker stats --no-stream                     # memory and CPU of each container
docker rm -f hello                           # window 1 shows kill, die, destroy
```

**4. Read-only look at the project's MongoDB:**

```powershell
docker logs seat-planner-mongo-1 --tail 5 -t
docker inspect seat-planner-mongo-1 --format "{{.State.Status}} since {{.State.StartedAt}}, restarts {{.RestartCount}}"
```

#### In this project

- **The API logs to stdout/stderr**, which is what Docker and Render expect. Startup prints
  `🚀 API listening on ...` ([`backend/src/server.js`](../../backend/src/server.js)); a failed start prints
  `❌ Failed to start server:` and exits with code 1, so the restart policy and Render both notice.
- **Request lines** come from `morgan("dev")`, switched on only outside production and tests
  ([`backend/src/app.js`](../../backend/src/app.js)). Every request also gets a `requestId`
  ([`backend/src/utils/requestContext.js`](../../backend/src/utils/requestContext.js)); today it ties a
  request's audit entries together, and it is ready to tag log lines the same way.
- **Graceful stop:** on SIGTERM the API stops its job worker and closes the server, with a 5-second
  backstop ([`backend/src/server.js`](../../backend/src/server.js)). The signal does get there: Alpine's
  `sh` hands its process number 1 (PID 1) over to the last command, so PID 1 is `npm start`, and npm passes
  SIGTERM on to Node. Checked with a copy of this setup: `docker stop` took about half a second and exited 0.
  If a container ever takes the whole grace period and ends in 137, the signal did not reach the app
  (see [`init`](#docker-security)).
- **Healthcheck:** MySQL's `mysqladmin ping` in [`docker-compose.yml`](../../docker-compose.yml), and the
  backend waits for `service_healthy`. Check it with
  `docker inspect seat-planner-db-1 --format "{{json .State.Health}}"`.
- **A real production incident:** the API on Render failed with `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND` for the database
  host. The logs said "cannot resolve the database's name"; the cause was that Aiven had powered the
  free database off after a period without use. Powering it on and redeploying fixed it. The lesson:
  read the first error in the log, not the last.
- **In production** the logs are in the Render dashboard (*Logs* tab) and the Vercel dashboard. The free
  Render plan has no shell, so `exec`-style debugging is not available there; logs are all you have,
  which is a good reason to log clearly.

#### At larger scale

Logs are shipped off the machine to a central store (Loki, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, CloudWatch,
Datadog) so they survive the container and can be searched across many of them. Kubernetes has the same
verbs: `kubectl logs`, `kubectl describe`, `kubectl exec`. See [Monitoring and logging](#part-4-monitoring-and-logging).

#### Common mistakes

- **Writing logs to a file inside the container.** Docker never sees them and they vanish with it. Log
  to stdout/stderr.
- **No log size limit.** `json-file` grows until the disk is full. Set it per service:
  `logging: { driver: json-file, options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" } }`.
- **Reading only the last line.** In a crash loop the useful error is usually the first one.
- **"It keeps restarting"** with a restart policy hides the crash. `docker ps -a` shows `Restarting (1)`;
  `docker inspect` shows `RestartCount`.
- **Debugging a container that is not the one running.** After a code change, rebuild
  (`docker compose up -d --build`), otherwise the old image is still running.
- **Printing secrets** in logs when dumping the environment to debug.

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "When a container misbehaves I go in a fixed order. `docker ps -a` tells me whether it is running,
> restarting or exited, and the exit code: 1 means the app itself failed, 137 means it was killed, often
> for memory, which `docker inspect` confirms with `OOMKilled`. Then `docker logs --tail 100` shows the
> last thing it printed, which is why our API logs to stdout and prints a clear line when it fails to
> start. If it is running, `docker exec -it ... sh` lets me look inside; if it dies too fast, I start the
> image with `--entrypoint sh` and run its command by hand.
>
> A real example: our API on Render logged `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND` for the database. That pointed
> straight at the database host, and the cause was Aiven had switched the free database off. Logs first,
> then the fix."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **The container exits immediately. What do you do?** `docker ps -a` for the exit code, `docker logs`
  for the message; if that is not enough, run the image with `--entrypoint sh` and start it by hand.
- **What does exit code 137 mean?** 128 + 9: it got SIGKILL. Either memory ran out (`OOMKilled: true`) or
  `docker stop` gave up waiting after 10 seconds.
- **Where are Docker's logs stored?** With the default `json-file` driver, in a JSON file per container
  on the Docker host (inside Docker Desktop's Linux machine on Windows). Use `docker logs`, not the file.
- **How do you stop logs filling the disk?** Log-rotation options (`max-size`, `max-file`) or a driver
  that ships logs elsewhere.
- **How do you see the environment a container was started with?**
  `docker inspect <name> --format "{{json .Config.Env}}"`, carefully, because it includes secrets.
- **How do you debug a failing `docker build`?** `docker build --progress=plain --no-cache .` shows every
  step's full output; then build up to the failing step and run the previous layer with `sh` to look around.

## Part 2: Docker, advanced

Goal: **App Deployment (Intermediate)**. Four sub-goals, all at 0%:
[Optimizing images](#optimizing-images), [Docker security](#docker-security),
[Resource management](#resource-management), [Custom registries](#custom-registries).

Read [Docker basics](#part-1-docker-basics) first; this part assumes `build`, `run`, `logs` and `inspect`.
Run the commands in **PowerShell** (see the note at the start of Part 1).

The numbers in this part were measured on this machine on 2026-11-15, by building the real
`backend/Dockerfile`. They will drift a little as dependencies change.

---

### Optimizing images

#### In one sentence

A good image contains only what the app needs to run, is built in an order that lets Docker reuse
earlier work, and is therefore small, fast to build and fast to start.

#### Why it matters

- **Speed.** Every deploy pushes and pulls the image. Smaller means faster deploys and faster scale-up.
  On Render's free plan the API sleeps when idle, so start-up time is something users feel.
- **Build time.** A build that reuses its cached dependency step takes seconds instead of minutes.
- **Security.** Every extra program in the image is something that can have a vulnerability. Less in it,
  less to patch.
- **Cost.** Registries and servers store every version you push.

#### Key ideas

| Idea | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **Base image** | Where the image starts. `node:20` (Debian, with compilers and tools) is about a gigabyte; `node:20-slim` is Debian without the extras; `node:20-alpine` is built on Alpine Linux, which is tiny. **Distroless** images go further: no shell, no package manager, only the runtime. |
| **Layer cache** | Docker reuses a step's result if that step and everything before it is unchanged. So put what changes **rarely** (installing dependencies) before what changes **often** (your code). |
| **Build context** | The folder you build from, sent to Docker in full. `.dockerignore` keeps `node_modules`, `.git` and `.env` out of it: faster, and no secrets in the image. |
| **Multi-stage build** | Several `FROM`s in one Dockerfile. An early stage has the compilers and dev tools and builds the app; the last stage copies **only the result**. The tools never reach the final image. |
| **Production dependencies only** | `npm ci --omit=dev` skips test and build tools. |
| **One layer, cleaned in the same step** | A file deleted in a *later* step still takes space in the earlier layer. Download, install and clean up in the **same** `RUN`. |
| **Inspecting** | `docker history <image>` lists each layer's size; the free tool `dive` lets you browse what is in each one. |

#### Try it yourself

```powershell
cd D:\Projects\seat-planner                      # the project folder
docker build -t sp-api:study backend             # first build: every step runs
docker build -t sp-api:study backend             # again: every step says CACHED, done in seconds
docker images sp-api                             # SIZE
docker history sp-api:study                      # one row per layer, with its size
docker run --rm --user root sp-api:study du -sh /root/.npm /app/node_modules
```

Now see the cache work for you: add a blank line to any file under `backend/src`, build again, and
note that `npm ci` is still `CACHED` and only `COPY . .` runs. Undo the blank line afterwards.

Clean up with `docker rmi sp-api:study`.

#### In this project

**[`backend/Dockerfile`](../../backend/Dockerfile)** already does the main things right, and says why in its comments:

- an Alpine base (`node:20-alpine`);
- `COPY package*.json` **before** `COPY . .`, so code changes do not reinstall dependencies;
- `npm ci --omit=dev` for production dependencies only;
- a `.dockerignore` ([`backend/.dockerignore`](../../backend/.dockerignore)) that leaves out `node_modules`
  (it is built for Windows and would break native modules in Linux), `.env` and `.git`.

What the measurement shows:

| Layer | Size |
|---|---|
| Node 20 on Alpine (the base) | about 220 MB |
| `npm ci --omit=dev` | 103 MB, of which **24 MB is npm's download cache** and 75 MB is `node_modules` |
| `COPY . .` (our code) | 3.9 MB, of which 1 MB is the `tests` folder |
| **Whole image** | **328 MB** |

**Two small improvements, not made yet** (the second one was built and measured):

1. Add `tests` to `.dockerignore`: tests do not need to ship.
2. Clean npm's cache in the same step: `RUN npm ci --omit=dev && npm cache clean --force`.
   **328 MB → 289 MB, about 12% smaller, for one line.**

**[`frontend/Dockerfile`](../../frontend/Dockerfile)** is a two-stage build. The `builder` stage installs
everything, including the Next.js compiler, and runs `npm run build`. The `runner` stage copies only
`.next/standalone` (a minimal server with just the modules it uses), `.next/static` and `public`. The
compiler and all dev dependencies stay behind in the discarded stage.

#### At larger scale

- **Distroless or "chiseled" images** (Google's `gcr.io/distroless/nodejs20`, Chainguard images): no
  shell at all. Smaller and safer, but you cannot `exec` into them to debug.
- **BuildKit cache mounts** keep npm's cache *between* builds without putting it in the image:
  `RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.npm npm ci --omit=dev`.
- **CI layer caching** (`cache-from` / `cache-to` with a registry or the GitHub Actions cache) so a fresh
  CI machine still reuses yesterday's layers.
- **Multi-platform builds** (`docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64`) for ARM servers.

#### Common mistakes

- `COPY . .` before `npm ci`: every code change reinstalls all dependencies.
- No `.dockerignore`: the host's `node_modules` and `.env` end up in the image.
- `RUN apt-get install ...` and then `RUN rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in a **separate** step: no saving.
- Installing dev dependencies in the final image.
- Chasing size at the cost of debuggability, then having no shell when production breaks. Decide on purpose.

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "Optimizing an image means it holds only what the app needs, built in an order Docker can cache. Our API
> image starts from Node 20 on Alpine, copies `package.json` first and installs production dependencies,
> then copies the code. A code change only redoes the last step, so a rebuild takes seconds.
>
> I measured it: 328 MB, of which our own code is 4 MB. The base is about 220 MB and dependencies 103 MB,
> and 24 MB of that is npm's cache, which serves no purpose at run time. Cleaning it in the same step brings
> the image to 289 MB, 12% smaller, for one line. The web image uses a multi-stage build: one stage has
> the compiler and builds, the final stage copies only Next.js's standalone output."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **Why copy `package.json` separately?** So the dependency layer is reused when only code changes.
- **What is a multi-stage build for?** To build with heavy tools and ship without them.
- **Alpine vs slim vs distroless?** Alpine is smallest with a shell, but uses `musl` instead of `glibc`, which
  occasionally breaks native modules. Slim is Debian, bigger but fewer surprises. Distroless is smallest
  in attack surface, with no shell.
- **Does deleting files in a later `RUN` make the image smaller?** No. Layers only add; delete in the same step.
- **How do you find what makes an image big?** `docker history`, or `dive` to browse each layer.

---

### Docker security

#### In one sentence

Keep the image small and up to date, run it as a normal user with no secrets inside, give the
container no more power or network access than it needs, and scan images for known vulnerabilities.

#### Why it matters

A container is not a virtual machine; it shares the host's kernel. If an attacker gets into the app,
everything the container is allowed to do, they can do: read its secrets, reach its networks, and, if it
runs as root with extra privileges, possibly the host itself.

#### Key ideas

| Idea | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **Non-root user** | By default a container runs as `root`. `USER node` makes it run as an ordinary user. |
| **No secrets in images** | Anyone who can pull an image can read every layer. Passwords and keys come in at run time as environment variables or secret files, never through `COPY` or `ARG`. |
| **Vulnerability scanning (CVEs)** | Tools compare the packages in an image against public lists of known flaws: `docker scout`, Trivy, Grype, Snyk. |
| **Patching by rebuilding** | You do not update a running container; you rebuild on the latest base image and redeploy. |
| **Least privilege for the container** | `cap_drop: [ALL]` removes Linux special powers, `read_only: true` makes the file system read-only, `no-new-privileges` stops a process from gaining more. |
| **Never `--privileged`, never mount `docker.sock`** | Either one hands the container control of the host. |
| **`init`** | A tiny first process (`docker run --init`, `init: true` in Compose) that passes signals on and cleans up finished child processes, for apps that cannot. |
| **Pin and verify** | Use exact tags or digests (`node:20-alpine@sha256:...`) and, where supported, signed images, so what you run is what you meant. |
| **Network exposure** | Publish only what must be public; keep databases on the private network. |

#### Try it yourself

```powershell
docker build -t sp-api:study D:\Projects\seat-planner\backend
docker run --rm sp-api:study id                                   # uid=1000(node): not root
docker run --rm --read-only sp-api:study sh -c "touch /app/x"     # Read-only file system
docker run --rm --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges sp-api:study node -v   # still runs fine

# Scan for HIGH and CRITICAL vulnerabilities (Trivy, run from its own container):
docker run --rm -v //var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock aquasec/trivy:0.58.1 image --scanners vuln --severity HIGH,CRITICAL sp-api:study
# Or, after `docker login`:  docker scout quickview sp-api:study
```

(Yes, the scanner is given `docker.sock`, the thing you must never give an app. A trusted tool you run
by hand on your own machine is the accepted exception; a long-running service is not.)

#### In this project

Done:

- **Both images run as a non-root user** (`USER node` in [`backend/Dockerfile`](../../backend/Dockerfile) and
  [`frontend/Dockerfile`](../../frontend/Dockerfile)). Checked: `id` prints `uid=1000(node)`.
- **No secrets in the images.** `.env` and `.env.*` are in both `.dockerignore` files; every secret
  (`JWT_SECRET`, database password, mail keys) is passed at run time by Compose or set in Render's dashboard.
- **Small, official base images** (`node:20-alpine`, `mysql:8`, `mongo:7`, `caddy:2-alpine`).
- **Only Caddy is published to the outside.** MySQL has no published port; MongoDB is published on
  127.0.0.1 only, with a comment explaining why ([`docker-compose.yml`](../../docker-compose.yml)).
- **The MySQL container uses a separate, non-root database user** for the app (`MYSQL_USER`), not root.
- **Signals reach the app** without an extra `init` process (checked; see
  [Docker basics](#debugging-and-logs)).

**What a scan found** (Trivy, HIGH and CRITICAL only, 2026-11-15): **49 findings, in three places**, and
each place is fixed a different way. That split is the main thing to learn from a scan:

| Where | Findings | How it is fixed |
|---|---|---|
| Alpine system packages (OpenSSL, musl, zlib) | 7 | Rebuild on a newer `node:20-alpine`; nothing to change in our code |
| The copy of **npm** inside the Node base image | 22 | npm is only needed to *install*; a multi-stage build (or a base without npm) leaves it out of the final image |
| **Our own dependencies** in `node_modules` | 20 | Update the packages; most fixes are within the version ranges `package.json` already allows |

No scan runs in CI today, so these were only found by looking. The fix for the third row is a normal
change to `master`, separate from these study notes.

Could be added, cheaply:

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml, per app service (backend, frontend)
    read_only: true
    tmpfs: [/tmp]
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
```

and a scan step in CI that fails the build on a CRITICAL finding.

#### At larger scale

- **Scanning in the pipeline and in the registry**: every pushed image is scanned, and the deploy is blocked
  on critical findings.
- **Signed images and policies**: images signed with Sigstore `cosign`; the cluster refuses unsigned ones.
- **SBOMs** (software bill of materials): a list of every package in the image, kept with it, so "are we
  affected by the new OpenSSL bug?" takes one search (`docker buildx build --sbom=true`).
- **Rootless Docker / user namespaces**: even "root" inside the container is an ordinary user on the host.
- **Runtime security tools** (Falco) that alert on unusual behaviour, such as a shell starting in a web container.
- **Secrets managers** (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Kubernetes Secrets) instead of plain environment variables.

#### Common mistakes

- Running as root because "it works".
- `COPY . .` without `.dockerignore`, shipping `.env`.
- Passing a secret as `ARG`: it is saved in the image history (`docker history` shows it).
- Never rebuilding: the base image's fixes never reach you.
- `ports: "3306:3306"` on a server.
- Mounting `/var/run/docker.sock` into a web app "for convenience".

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "A container shares the host's kernel, so container security is about limiting what an attacker gets if
> they break into the app. Our images start from small official bases, run as the `node` user rather than
> root, and contain no secrets: `.env` is excluded, and every secret is given at run time. Only the Caddy
> proxy has public ports; MySQL is not published at all and MongoDB only on the loopback address.
>
> What I would add: a read-only file system and dropped capabilities in Compose, and an image scan in CI.
> I scanned the API image with Trivy: the findings came from three places: Alpine's own packages, the copy
> of npm in the Node base image, and our dependencies. Each is fixed differently: rebuild on a newer base,
> leave npm out of the final image, update our packages. Patching a container always means rebuilding and
> redeploying, never changing it in place."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **Why not run as root inside a container?** If the app is compromised, root inside plus a kernel or
  configuration flaw can mean root on the host. A normal user removes that step.
- **How do you pass secrets to a container?** Environment variables or mounted secret files at run time,
  ideally from a secrets manager. Never in the image.
- **What is a CVE?** A public ID for a known vulnerability (`CVE-2025-66478` was the Next.js one this
  project upgraded for). Scanners match your packages against these lists.
- **What does `--privileged` do?** Gives the container nearly all the host's powers. Avoid it.
- **How do you keep images patched?** Rebuild regularly on the latest base (pinned to a version, not
  `latest`), let a bot like Dependabot or Renovate propose base-image updates, and scan.

---

### Resource management

#### In one sentence

Limit how much memory, CPU and other resources each container may use, so one misbehaving container
cannot starve the rest, and size those limits from what the app really uses.

#### Why it matters

By default a container may use **all** the memory and CPU of the machine (on Windows: of Docker
Desktop's Linux VM, 3.7 GB here). A memory leak in one service then slows or kills every service on the
host. Limits turn "the whole server froze" into "one container restarted".

#### Key ideas

| Idea | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **Memory limit** | `-m 512m`. If the container goes over, the kernel kills it: exit code 137, `OOMKilled: true`. |
| **Memory reservation** | A soft floor the container is guaranteed when memory is tight. |
| **CPU limit** | `--cpus 1.5` = at most one and a half CPU cores' worth of time. Going over **slows** the container down; it is not killed. |
| **CPU shares** | A relative weight, used only when CPUs are busy: 2048 gets twice the time of 1024. |
| **PIDs limit** | `--pids-limit 200`: the most processes it may start. Stops a runaway loop from exhausting the host. |
| **cgroups** | The Linux kernel feature that enforces all of these. |
| **Disk** | Logs (no limit by default), volumes and old images all fill disks. Rotate logs, prune images. |
| **Limits for the app inside** | Node decides its heap size itself. Set `NODE_OPTIONS=--max-old-space-size=...` a little below the container limit (about 75%), so Node cleans up harder before the kernel kills it. |
| **Connections are resources too** | A database accepts only so many connections. A connection pool caps how many the app opens. |

#### Try it yourself

```powershell
docker run -d --name capped -m 64m --cpus 0.5 nginx:alpine
docker run -d --name busy --cpus 0.5 alpine sh -c "while :; do :; done"   # spins one CPU as hard as it can
docker stats --no-stream            # busy ~50% CPU (its cap), capped shows "/ 64MiB" as its memory limit
docker update --memory 128m --memory-swap 128m capped    # change a limit on a running container
docker stats --no-stream capped     # now "/ 128MiB"
docker rm -f capped busy
```

And the out-of-memory kill, from Part 1:

```powershell
docker run --name oom -m 32m alpine sh -c "tail /dev/zero"
docker inspect oom --format "{{.State.ExitCode}} OOMKilled={{.State.OOMKilled}}"   # 137 OOMKilled=true
docker rm oom
```

#### In this project

- **No container limits are set** in [`docker-compose.yml`](../../docker-compose.yml) today. For a
  single small server, a sensible start would be:

  ```yaml
  # docker-compose.yml, per service
    backend:
      deploy:
        resources:
          limits:   { cpus: "1.0", memory: 512M }
          reservations: { memory: 256M }
      environment:
        NODE_OPTIONS: --max-old-space-size=384
      logging:
        driver: json-file
        options: { max-size: "10m", max-file: "3" }
  ```

  The numbers should come from `docker stats` under real load, not guesses.
- **In production the platform sets the limits.** Render's free plan gives the API a small memory and
  CPU allowance (check Render's pricing page for the current figures) and restarts it if it goes over;
  Vercel limits each server function's memory and run time.
- **The database connection pool is resource management.** Sequelize's pool is capped by `DB_POOL_MAX`
  (default 10, [`backend/src/config/database.js`](../../backend/src/config/database.js)); production runs
  with **3**, because Aiven's free MySQL allows only a few connections. Without the cap a traffic burst
  would open more connections than the database accepts, and requests would fail.
- **Other built-in limits:** a request-rate limit on the public Seat Allocation API
  ([`backend/src/utils/rateLimiter.js`](../../backend/src/utils/rateLimiter.js)), a sign-in lockout after
  too many wrong passwords ([`backend/src/services/authService.js`](../../backend/src/services/authService.js)),
  and every email send gives up after 15 seconds
  ([`backend/src/services/emailService.js`](../../backend/src/services/emailService.js)) so a stuck mail
  server cannot hold requests open.

#### At larger scale

- **Kubernetes `requests` and `limits`** per container: the scheduler places containers by their
  requests and enforces the limits. Pods without them are first to be evicted.
- **Autoscaling**: add containers when CPU or request rate is high (Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, ECS
  service auto-scaling), remove them when quiet.
- **Quotas per team or namespace**, so one team cannot use the whole cluster.
- **Right-sizing** from monitoring data (see [Monitoring and logging](#part-4-monitoring-and-logging)).

#### Common mistakes

- **No limits at all.** One leak takes down the host.
- **Limits too tight.** The container is killed with 137 under normal load; it looks like a random crash.
- **A memory limit without telling Node.** Node's heap may grow past the limit and get killed instead of
  collecting garbage.
- **Treating a CPU limit like a memory limit.** Over the CPU limit you are slowed, not killed; slow
  responses may be throttling.
- **Forgetting disk.** Unrotated logs and old images fill the disk; then everything fails at once.

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "Without limits a container can use all the memory and CPU on the machine, so one leak takes everything
> down. Docker lets me cap memory, where going over gets the container killed with exit code 137, and CPU,
> where going over just slows it down. I tested both: a container capped at half a CPU sits at 50% even when
> it spins as hard as it can, and one capped at 32 MB is killed and flagged `OOMKilled`.
>
> Our Compose file has no limits yet; I would add about 512 MB and one CPU for the API, tell Node its heap
> limit, and rotate logs. In production Render enforces limits for us. And resource management is not only
> Docker: our MySQL connection pool is capped at 3 in production because Aiven's free plan allows only a few
> connections."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **What happens when a container hits its memory limit?** The kernel's OOM killer stops it: exit 137,
  `OOMKilled: true`. With a restart policy it starts again.
- **And its CPU limit?** It is throttled, never killed.
- **How do you choose the numbers?** Measure normal and peak use (`docker stats`, monitoring), set the
  limit with some headroom, then watch for OOM kills and throttling.
- **Do limits in `deploy:` work outside Swarm?** Yes, with Docker Compose v2 `limits` are applied.
- **What else besides CPU and memory?** Processes (`--pids-limit`), disk (log rotation, prune), open files,
  and outside resources such as database connections.

---

### Custom registries

#### In one sentence

A registry is a server that stores and serves images; a custom (private) registry is one your team
controls, so your own images are kept private, close to your servers, and scanned and cleaned up on your terms.

#### Why it matters

`docker pull` uses Docker Hub by default, which is public and limits how often anonymous users may pull.
Your own app's images usually must not be public, should be close to where they run, and should be
**built once, then deployed many times**: the same image that passed the tests goes to staging and to
production, which needs a place to keep it.

#### Key ideas

| Idea | In plain words |
|---|---|
| **Image name anatomy** | `registry.example.com:5000/team/app:1.4.2`: registry host, then repository path, then tag. No host means Docker Hub. |
| **Tag vs digest** | A tag (`1.4.2`) is a label that can be moved to a new image. A digest (`@sha256:...`) is the image's fingerprint and never changes. |
| **Push / pull** | `docker tag` gives an image the registry's name; `docker push` uploads it; `docker pull` downloads it. |
| **Login** | `docker login <host>`. On Windows the password is kept in Windows Credential Manager. CI uses short-lived tokens, not a person's password. |
| **Hosted registries** | Docker Hub (private repositories), **GitHub Container Registry** (`ghcr.io`), AWS ECR, Google Artifact Registry, Azure Container Registry, GitLab's registry. |
| **Self-hosted registries** | `registry:2` (the basic open-source one), **Harbor** (adds users, scanning, replication), Nexus, Artifactory. |
| **Pull-through cache / mirror** | A local registry that keeps copies of Docker Hub images, to avoid rate limits and speed up pulls. |
| **Retention and immutability** | Rules that delete old images, and that forbid overwriting a tag once pushed. |

#### Try it yourself

Run a registry on your own machine, push an image to it, delete it locally and pull it back:

```powershell
docker run -d --name registry -p 127.0.0.1:5000:5000 registry:2
docker build -t sp-api:study D:\Projects\seat-planner\backend
docker tag sp-api:study localhost:5000/seat-planner-api:1.0.0     # same image, a registry name
docker push localhost:5000/seat-planner-api:1.0.0
curl.exe http://localhost:5000/v2/_catalog                        # {"repositories":["seat-planner-api"]}
curl.exe http://localhost:5000/v2/seat-planner-api/tags/list      # {"name":"seat-planner-api","tags":["1.0.0"]}
docker rmi localhost:5000/seat-planner-api:1.0.0
docker pull localhost:5000/seat-planner-api:1.0.0                 # comes back from your registry
docker images --digests localhost:5000/seat-planner-api           # the sha256 digest
docker rm -f -v registry                                          # -v also removes its storage
docker rmi localhost:5000/seat-planner-api:1.0.0 sp-api:study
```

(`localhost` is the one address Docker lets you use without HTTPS. Any other registry host needs TLS.)

#### In this project

- **No registry of our own is used today.** Render builds `backend/Dockerfile` straight from the Git
  repository on every deploy, and Vercel builds the web app from source. The only images pulled are
  official ones from Docker Hub: `node:20-alpine`, `mysql:8`, `mongo:7`, `caddy:2-alpine`.
- **What a registry would change**, as a worked design:
  1. CI builds the API image **once** per merge to `master`, tags it with the commit's ID, and pushes it to
     GitHub Container Registry: `ghcr.io/<owner>/seat-planner-api:<commit>`.
  2. Render deploys **that image** (it supports deploying an existing image) instead of rebuilding.
  3. The image that passed CI is exactly the image in production; **rolling back** is choosing the previous
     tag (see [Rollback and disaster recovery](#part-5-rollback-and-disaster-recovery)).

  The CI part would be a few lines in [`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](../../.github/workflows/ci.yml):

  ```yaml
  # a new job, after the tests pass on master
    image:
      needs: [backend]
      if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/master'
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      permissions: { contents: read, packages: write }    # the token may push packages, nothing more
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        - uses: docker/login-action@v3
          with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: "${{ github.actor }}", password: "${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}" }
        - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
          with:
            context: backend
            push: true
            tags: ghcr.io/${{ github.repository_owner }}/seat-planner-api:${{ github.sha }}
  ```

#### At larger scale

- One registry per company (Harbor, Artifactory or a cloud registry), with **projects per team**, access
  rules, **scanning on push**, **signing**, and **replication** to registries near each region.
- **Promotion**: an image moves from `dev` to `staging` to `prod` repositories by copying the same digest,
  never by rebuilding.
- **Retention policies**: keep the last N images per branch, keep every release forever.
- **Mirrors** for Docker Hub so builds do not hit its pull limits.

#### Common mistakes

- Pushing private images to a **public** Docker Hub repository.
- Deploying `:latest`: you cannot tell which version runs or roll back to "the previous latest".
- Overwriting a tag (`1.4.2`) with a different image. Make tags immutable.
- Using a person's password in CI instead of a token with only the rights it needs.
- No cleanup: the registry grows forever and costs money.

#### Explain it in two minutes

> "A registry stores images. Docker Hub is the public default; a custom registry is one we control, such as
> GitHub Container Registry, a cloud registry, or a self-hosted one like Harbor. An image's name says where
> it lives, `ghcr.io/owner/app:tag`, and its digest is a fingerprint that never changes.
>
> I ran one locally: `registry:2` on port 5000, tagged our API image for it, pushed it, deleted it from my
> machine and pulled it back. Today this project does not use one: Render builds from Git on every deploy.
> With a registry, CI would build the image once, tag it with the commit, and Render would deploy exactly that
> image, so what we tested is what runs, and a rollback is just picking the previous tag."

#### Questions you may be asked

- **Why not just use Docker Hub?** You can, with private repositories. Teams choose others to be close to
  their cloud, for access control tied to their organisation, for scanning, or to avoid pull limits.
- **Tag or digest for deploys?** A unique tag (like the commit ID) for people to read; the digest for the
  strongest guarantee. Never `latest`.
- **How does CI log in safely?** A short-lived token with only push rights to that repository, such as
  GitHub's built-in `GITHUB_TOKEN` with `packages: write`.
- **What is Harbor?** An open-source registry that adds users and projects, vulnerability scanning,
  signing and replication on top of the basic registry.
- **How do you clean up old images?** Retention rules in the registry (keep last N, delete untagged), and
  `docker image prune` on build machines.

## Part 3: Security in application deployment

Goal: **App Deployment (Intermediate)**, sub-goal *Security in Application Deployment* (0%).

Container-specific security (non-root images, scanning, capabilities) is in
[Docker, advanced](#docker-security). This part is the wider picture: everything
between a developer's commit and a request being answered in production.

The checks marked *(checked 2026-11-15)* were run against this repository and the live site on that day,
read-only.

---

### In one sentence

Deployment security means protecting every step from code to running service (the code and its
dependencies, the build, the secrets, the network path, the running app, and the people with access),
so that one weak step does not open the rest.

### Why it matters

Most real breaches are not clever attacks on the code. They are a secret committed to Git, a database left
open to the internet, an old library with a known flaw, an over-powered CI token, or a test environment
wired to real data. Each is a deployment decision, not an application bug.

### Key ideas

Think of it as layers. An attacker has to get through all of them; each one you add is called
**defence in depth**.

| Layer | What to protect | The usual tools |
|---|---|---|
| **Code and dependencies** (the *supply chain*) | Third-party packages with known flaws, or malicious ones | Lock files (`package-lock.json`, `npm ci`), `npm audit`, Dependabot or Renovate, image scanning |
| **Build and CI** | The pipeline can deploy to production, so it is a target | Least-privilege tokens, protected branches, required reviews and checks, pinned versions of CI actions |
| **Secrets** | Passwords, signing keys, API keys | Never in Git or images; injected at run time from the platform's secret store or a secrets manager; rotated |
| **Transport** | Data on the wire | HTTPS everywhere (TLS), HSTS so browsers never fall back to HTTP, TLS to the database with certificate checks |
| **Network** | What can be reached at all | Only the entry point is public; databases private or IP-restricted; firewalls |
| **The running app** | Requests themselves | Authentication, authorization (permissions), input validation, CORS allow-list, rate limits, bot checks, security headers, no stack traces to users |
| **People and access** | Accounts on GitHub, Vercel, Render, Aiven | Two-factor sign-in, fewest people with production access, separate accounts, no shared passwords |
| **Data** | What is stored | Hashed passwords, encryption at rest (managed DBs do this), backups, separate test data |
| **Detection** | Knowing something happened | Audit trail, logs, alerts (see [Monitoring and logging](#part-4-monitoring-and-logging)) |

Some terms you will hear:

- **Least privilege**: every account, token and container gets only the rights it needs.
- **Shift left**: catch problems early (in the editor or in CI), not in production.
- **SAST / DAST**: *static* analysis reads the code for flaws; *dynamic* testing attacks the running app (for example OWASP ZAP).
- **OWASP Top 10**: the standard list of the most common web app weaknesses (broken access control, injection, and so on).
- **CVE**: a public ID for a known vulnerability.
- **CORS**: the browser rule that decides which *other websites* may call your API from their pages.
- **HSTS**: a header telling browsers "only ever use HTTPS for this site".

### Try it yourself

```powershell
cd D:\Projects\seat-planner\backend
npm audit --omit=dev                     # known flaws in the production dependencies

# The live site's security headers (read-only):
curl.exe -sI https://seat-planner-sable.vercel.app/login
curl.exe -sI https://seat-planner-api.onrender.com/api/v1/health

# Does the API answer a page from another website? (CORS)
curl.exe -s -D - -o NUL -H "Origin: https://seat-planner-sable.vercel.app" https://seat-planner-api.onrender.com/api/v1/health
curl.exe -s -D - -o NUL -H "Origin: https://evil.example" https://seat-planner-api.onrender.com/api/v1/health

# Scan the whole Git history for committed secrets (shows findings with the secret hidden):
docker run --rm -v "D:/Projects/seat-planner:/repo" zricethezav/gitleaks:v8.21.2 git /repo --redact --no-banner
```

What to look for: in the headers, `Strict-Transport-Security` (good) and `X-Powered-By` (tells an
attacker the framework; better hidden). In the CORS test, the first answer carries
`access-control-allow-origin`, the second does not.

### In this project

**Secrets**

- `.env` is in [`.gitignore`](../../.gitignore) and both `.dockerignore` files; only `.env.example` (no
  real values) is committed. Production secrets live in Render's and Vercel's settings.
- *(checked)* A gitleaks scan of the whole Git history found **16 "possible secrets", all false positives**:
  seat-plan keys such as `EKOTA-CABIN-48` and a deliberately fake token in a test. This is normal; scanners
  are cautious, and someone has to look. Real teams record reviewed false positives in a `.gitleaksignore`.
- CI uses a throw-away `JWT_SECRET: ci-only-secret` and a database that exists only for that run
  ([`.github/workflows/ci.yml`](../../.github/workflows/ci.yml)).

**Transport**

- *(checked)* The web app redirects HTTP to HTTPS (`308`) and sends **HSTS** with a two-year `max-age`
  (Vercel does this). The API is HTTPS-only on Render.
- Self-hosted, Caddy gets and renews a certificate automatically ([`Caddyfile`](../../Caddyfile)).
- The connection to Aiven MySQL is encrypted (`DB_SSL=true`). **But** the certificate is not verified by
  default, because no CA file is shipped
  ([`backend/src/config/database.js`](../../backend/src/config/database.js), lines 5-9): encrypted, but a
  machine in the middle could pose as the database. The fix is to ship Aiven's CA certificate and set
  `DB_SSL_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=true`.

**Network**

- Self-hosted: only Caddy is published; MySQL is not reachable from outside and MongoDB only from the
  machine itself ([`docker-compose.yml`](../../docker-compose.yml)).
- In production the database is a managed service reached over TLS with a password.

**The running app**

- **Passwords** are hashed with bcrypt (`bcryptjs`), and repeated wrong passwords pause sign-in for that
  email address for a configurable time ([`backend/src/services/authService.js`](../../backend/src/services/authService.js)).
- **Routes check permissions** ([`backend/src/middleware/authorize.js`](../../backend/src/middleware/authorize.js)),
  and **input is validated** before it reaches the services
  ([`backend/src/middleware/validate.js`](../../backend/src/middleware/validate.js)).
- **CORS allow-list** ([`backend/src/utils/allowedOrigin.js`](../../backend/src/utils/allowedOrigin.js)):
  only the listed origins, with a careful `*` that matches one piece of a host name and never a dot, so
  `seat-planner-x.evil.com` cannot pass as a Vercel preview. *(checked)* The live API answers the real site
  with `access-control-allow-origin` and refuses another origin. The refusal currently comes back as a
  `500` error rather than a `403`: safe, but untidy, and it writes an error to the log each time.
- **The public Seat Allocation API** only answers through the web app: the app proves it with a shared
  `PUBLIC_EDGE_SECRET`, compared in constant time so the comparison's timing does not leak it
  ([`backend/src/utils/publicRequest.js`](../../backend/src/utils/publicRequest.js)); it is rate-limited and
  can require a Cloudflare Turnstile bot check.
- **No stack traces in production:** the error handler adds the stack only outside production, and only
  our own error codes are passed on, never system ones such as `ECONNREFUSED`
  ([`backend/src/middleware/errorHandler.js`](../../backend/src/middleware/errorHandler.js)).
- **Audit trail:** sensitive actions are recorded in MongoDB
  ([`backend/src/services/auditService.js`](../../backend/src/services/auditService.js)). For the
  subscription check API the record keeps the reason, while the caller only ever sees *valid: false*.

**Supply chain**

- `npm ci` installs exactly what `package-lock.json` says, in CI and in the image.
- Next.js was upgraded for **CVE-2025-66478** when it was announced: the textbook response.
- No automatic check yet: there is no Dependabot and no scan in CI, and the image scan on
  [Docker, advanced](#docker-security) found dependency updates waiting.

**Gaps worth saying out loud**

| Gap | Why it matters | The fix |
|---|---|---|
| Vercel **preview deployments use the production API and data** | Anyone testing a branch works on real data | A separate staging API and database for previews |
| Database certificate not verified | Encrypted, but open to impersonation | Ship the CA, set `DB_SSL_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED=true` |
| API has no security headers (`X-Powered-By: Express` is visible) | Small, but free to fix | `app.disable("x-powered-by")` and the `helmet` middleware |
| No dependency or image scan in CI | Known flaws arrive unnoticed | Dependabot, plus `npm audit --audit-level=high` or Trivy as a CI step |
| `ci.yml` does not set `permissions:` | The CI token gets the repository default | `permissions: { contents: read }` at the top, as `android.yml` already does for its job |

### At larger scale

- **Secrets managers** (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) with automatic rotation and
  an audit log of who read what.
- **Single sign-on and short-lived credentials**: engineers get temporary production access when needed
  and it expires; CI authenticates to the cloud with OpenID Connect instead of stored keys.
- **Policy as code**: rules like "no public databases" or "images must be signed" checked automatically.
- **A web application firewall (WAF)** and DDoS protection in front of the app (Cloudflare, AWS WAF).
- **Separate environments and accounts**: development, staging and production cannot reach each other's data.
- **Regular penetration tests** and a security review in the release process.

### Common mistakes

- Committing `.env`, or a key "just for a minute". Git keeps it forever; rotate the key, do not just delete the file.
- Test or preview environments connected to production data.
- `CORS: *` together with cookies or tokens.
- One admin account shared by the team; no two-factor sign-in.
- Error pages that show stack traces or SQL.
- A CI token or cloud key with full admin rights.
- Updating dependencies only when something breaks.
- Treating HTTPS to the browser as "done" while the database connection is unverified.

### Explain it in two minutes

> "Deployment security is about every step from commit to production, because most breaches come from a
> leaked secret, an open database or an old library, not from clever attacks.
>
> In this project: secrets never enter Git or the images; they live in Render's and Vercel's settings. I
> scanned the whole history with gitleaks: sixteen hits, all false positives, like seat-plan keys. The site
> forces HTTPS and sends HSTS; the API allows only our own origins through CORS, which I checked live; every
> route checks permissions and validates input; passwords are bcrypt-hashed with a lockout; errors never
> show stack traces in production; and sensitive actions go to an audit trail.
>
> And I would be upfront about what is missing: preview deployments share production data, the database
> certificate is not verified, and nothing scans dependencies automatically. Each has a small, known fix."

### Questions you may be asked

- **Where should secrets live?** In the platform's secret settings or a secrets manager, injected at run
  time. Never in Git, images, logs, or front-end code.
- **A secret was committed. What now?** Rotate it first (it is already compromised), then remove it from
  history if needed, then add scanning so it does not happen again.
- **What is least privilege?** Every user, token and service gets only the access it needs, so one
  compromise stays small.
- **What does CORS protect, and what does it not?** It stops *other websites' pages* from calling your API
  through a visitor's browser. It does not stop scripts or servers calling the API directly; that is what
  authentication and rate limits are for.
- **What is HSTS?** A response header telling browsers to use only HTTPS for the site, for a set time, so
  a downgrade to HTTP is not possible.
- **How do you keep dependencies safe?** Lock files and `npm ci`, automated update pull requests, a scan in
  CI that fails on high-severity findings, and acting quickly on announced CVEs.
- **Why separate staging from production?** So testing cannot damage or expose real data, and a bad change
  is caught before customers see it.
